name: Tanzania
sources: GDP $4.3bn and 25.5m people (World Bank, 1990). Among the poorest recorded dollar incomes on earth at the start date, and the ratio to Kenya next door — half the output for more people — is the twenty-five-year experiment this file is describing.

Inflation 35.8% (Bureau of Statistics Dar es Salaam CPI, 1990). Interest 31%: the Bank of Tanzania was raising administered rates toward positive real territory under the IMF programme and had not got there.
Public and publicly guaranteed debt 1.20 of GDP. Tanzania's external debt was roughly $6.5bn against a $4.3bn economy and effectively unpayable; it entered HIPC on those grounds a decade later.

Command system: the Arusha Declaration of 1967 and the leadership code were still formally in force in January 1990 and were only repudiated by the Zanzibar Declaration of February 1991. Roughly 400 parastatals held the commanding heights and villagisation had moved most of the rural population. The Economic Recovery Programme had been liberalising prices and trade since 1986, so this is a command economy in retreat rather than at its height.
Defence 3.2% of GDP for about 45,000 personnel — high for the income, and the legacy of the 1978-79 Uganda war that removed Amin at a cost Tanzania financed alone and never recovered.

Authoritarianism 0.79 and stability 55: Chama Cha Mapinduzi was the sole legal party and Article 3 of the constitution said so. Nyerere handed the CCM chairmanship to President Mwinyi in August 1990, and the Nyalali Commission that recommended multipartism reported in 1991. Legitimacy was unusually high for a one-party state, which is why stability sits well above Kenya's.

Separatism 0.22: the Union question. Zanzibar has its own president, legislature and constitution under the 1964 articles of union, and the demand for a distinct Tanganyikan government inside a three-tier federation was live and remains so.
Military strength 3: infantry mass with obsolescent Chinese equipment and no projection beyond a neighbouring border.
